titel: Agar, alginate, carrageenan: setting without gelatine
kurz: Many gelling and thickening agents come from seaweed, seeds or bacteria. They are long sugar chains that trap water, and each has its own rules: some need heat, some need calcium, some can't take acid.
bild_im_kopf: Like different keys for the same lock: all of them lock water in, but each one turns differently.
was_passiert: [[gelatine|Gelatine]] is protein from collagen and melts at body temperature. [[agar-agar|Agar]] from red seaweed has to boil, sets at around 40 °C and only melts again around 85 °C. Alginate from brown seaweed sets cold as soon as it meets calcium. A drop in calcium water gets a thin skin this way (spherification). Carrageenan comes in firm and soft types, while locust bean and guar gum thicken without setting.
warum_wichtig: Knowing what each agent needs lets you replace gelatine with a vegetarian option or make jellies you can serve warm. And you understand why a recipe with pineapple or lemon juice didn't set.
faustregeln: For jellies served warm: agar, because it only melts again around 85 °C.
Boil agar for at least two minutes, otherwise it won't set.
For spherification: about 0.5 % alginate in the liquid and a bath of about 0.5 % calcium chloride, guide values from modernist cooking.
Very acidic liquids set poorly with alginate, because it clumps below a pH of about 3.6.
Amounts vary a lot between products: the packet instructions come first.
